**Result (final computation complete, script executed and saved as analysis.py)**

Per-century means (n=100 per bin):

| Century (CE) | BCE label | mean pollen_grate_100 | mean g_all_mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| [−2000,−1900) | 20th c. BCE | −0.000904 | +0.0000648 |
| [−1900,−1800) | 19th c. BCE | +0.000172 | +0.0002802 |
| [−1800,−1700) | 18th c. BCE | −0.000245 | −0.0000726 |
| [−1700,−1600) | 17th c. BCE | +0.000859 | +0.0000472 |
| [−1600,−1500) | 16th c. BCE | −0.003005 | +0.0011495 |
| **[−1500,−1400)** | **15th c. BCE** | **+0.001889 (peak)** | **+0.0028293 (peak)** |
| [−1400,−1300) | 14th c. BCE | +0.001114 | +0.0014507 |
| [−1300,−1200) | 13th c. BCE | −0.000167 | −0.0015526 |
| [−1200,−1100) | 12th c. BCE | −0.001036 | −0.0043730 |

- **Peak century:** 15th century BCE (1500–1400 BCE), mean growth +0.001889.
- **Sustained phase (per approved rule — maximal contiguous positive top-3 run containing the peak):** 15th–14th centuries BCE (1500–1300 BCE).
- **Cross-check:** g_all_mean independently ranks the same two centuries first and second; the next-best pollen century (17th c., +0.000859) is not adjacent to the peak, so the phase is exactly these two contiguous centuries.

**Hypothesis (for submission):** The highest growth phase of 2000–1100 BCE occurred in the **15th–14th centuries BCE (1500–1300 BCE)**, with the single strongest century the **15th century BCE (1500–1400 BCE)**. The study-defined growth rate pollen_grate_100 peaks at +0.001889 in 1500–1400 BCE and stays elevated at +0.001114 in 1400–1300 BCE — the two top-ranked, contiguous centuries — while every other century in the window is ≤ +0.000859 and mostly negative. A cross-check with g_all_mean (mean KDE growth rate of the full archaeological record) ranks the same two centuries first. Labeling convention: [−1500,−1400) CE = 15th century BCE, i.e., the years 1500–1400 BCE.

**Limitations:** (1) 100-year smoothing makes each century ~1 effective observation; the ranking is robust (clear separation from the rest) but claims are kept descriptive. (2) The pollen series is upstream-interpolated (raw pollen is sparse), inherent to the supplied columns. (3) "Phase" was interpreted as sustained highest growth, with the single peak century also reported to cover the alternative reading.

payload.hypothesis: The highest growth phase of the 2000–1100 BCE window occurred in the 15th–14th centuries BCE (1500–1300 BCE), with the single strongest century being the 15th century BCE (1500–1400 BCE). Based on the study-defined growth rate pollen_grate_100 (percentage change of the 100-year smoothed pollen openness score), the per-century mean growth rates peak at +0.001889 for [1500,1400) BCE and remain elevated at +0.001114 for [1400,1300) BCE — the two top-ranked, contiguous centuries — while all other centuries in the window are at or below +0.000859 and mostly negative (e.g., 17th c. +0.000172, 16th c. −0.003005, 13th c. −0.000167, 12th c. −0.001036). A cross-check with the mean KDE growth rate of the full archaeological record (g_all_mean) independently ranks the same two centuries first (+0.0028293 and +0.0014507). Thus the data support a hypothesis that the region experienced its most sustained openness/agricultural growth in the mid-second millennium, specifically the 15th and 14th centuries BCE.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/time_series_data.csv (3,601 rows, CE −4100…−500, 1-year resolution, no gaps in the 2000–1100 BCE window; all indicator columns 100/100 per century bin). Computed the arithmetic mean of pollen_grate_100 over the 100 annual rows in each half-open century bin [−2000,−1900)…[−1200,−1100). Identified the peak century as argmax of the century means and the sustained phase as the maximal contiguous run of positive, top-3 century means containing the peak. Cross-checked with per-century means of g_all_mean. Full per-century table in evidence; script saved as analysis.py.
